nuance.usage_note: Americans mutter when they are annoyed or talking half to themselves, as in 'He muttered something about traffic.' The word describes how something is said more than what is said. If someone mutters, you can reply 'What?' or 'Say that again?' Do not use mutter for speaking clearly or loudly.

distinctions.note: Whisper means speaking very softly but still clearly; mutter means speaking unclearly, often in complaint.
Grumble is low, discontented complaining, often without clear words; mutter involves indistinct words.

examples.everyday: He muttered something about the coffee being cold.
examples.professional: She muttered a quick sounds fine during the call, so I wasn't sure she actually agreed.
examples.analytical: Her objection came as a muttered aside, which made it easy to dismiss rather than debate.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio playing in another room: you hear the sound and rhythm, but not the words.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of low, indistinct sound, related to Middle Low German mutteren.
common_mistakes: Using mutter to mean speak clearly or formally
Confusing mutter with mumble, which is more about slurred speech
nuance.biblical_note: In Isaiah 8:19 (RSV) people are told to consult mediums and wizards who chirp and mutter, a rebuke of seeking guidance from the dead instead of from God. The Hebrew verbs there are rendered in different ways, so the English reflects translators' choices. Isaiah 29:4 describes a humbled city whose speech comes faintly from the dust, a related image of faint, indistinct speech.

senses.definition: Initialism of most valuable player.
Initialism of most vexing parse.
Initialism of minimum viable product.
Initialism of model-view-presenter.
Initialism of model view projection.
Initialism of minimum viable population.
Initialism of mitral valve prolapse.

core.definition: Most valuable player: the player voted or named as the best and most important in a season, a game or a team.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters as separate letters, with the strongest stress on PEE. The American pronunciation does not sound like a single word such as 'em-vip.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a player's excellence and importance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use MVP constantly in sports conversations, sports news and fan talk. It is usually said as the letters 'em-vee-pee.' Outside sports, people sometimes use 'MVP' jokingly to mean the person who helped the most, which is informal. Use it with the sport or award name when clarity matters, such as 'league MVP.'

distinctions.note: A star is a highly skilled or famous player, while the MVP is the player judged most valuable to a team's success.
An all-star is selected for an exhibition game based on popularity and performance, while the MVP is an award given for the season or event.

examples.everyday: Did you see who got Super Bowl MVP last year? He was amazing.
examples.professional: My team said our marketing lead was the MVP of the product launch because she kept everyone on schedule.
examples.analytical: The MVP award often rewards overall impact rather than individual statistics alone, which makes its criteria contested.

nuance.analogy: The MVP is like the keystone of an arch: it may not be the largest stone, but the structure depends on it most.
nuance.etymology: An initialism of most valuable player, formed in English from the three words.
common_mistakes: Saying 'MVP' as a single word, like 'em-vip'; Americans say the three letters separately.
Using MVP for any good player; the word means the top player in an award or season.

conversation.text: He was the MVP of the Super Bowl last year.
Who do you think will win MVP this season?
You brought the extra chairs? You're the MVP today.

senses.definition: A woman named in Genesis as the daughter of Lamech and sister of Tubal-cain, and another woman named as Solomon's Ammonite wife.

core.definition: A woman named in Genesis as the daughter of Lamech and sister of Tubal-cain, and another woman named as Solomon's Ammonite wife.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final two syllables are weak, both reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a Hebrew personal name used only in Bible discussion, study or church settings. Americans would say it as a proper name without any special emphasis, and it has no everyday meaning.

distinctions.note: Naaman is a Syrian army commander healed of leprosy, while Naamah is a woman; the names are similar but unrelated.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study group, someone asked who Naamah was, and we found her in Genesis 4.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan on Genesis genealogies, I include Naamah as one of the few named women in the early chapters.
examples.analytical: The Genesis 4 genealogy names Naamah among Lamech's descendants, a detail that some commentators read as a sign of women's presence in early culture.

nuance.analogy: Like a minor character in a long family tree, she is named briefly but is part of the record.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Na'amah, often understood as 'pleasant' or 'lovely,' though the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing her with Naaman, the Syrian commander.
Stressing the second syllable as 'nay-AH-muh.'
nuance.biblical_note: Naamah (Hebrew Na'amah, possibly 'pleasant') appears in Genesis 4:22 as the daughter of Lamech and sister of Tubal-cain, a metalworker. In 1 Kings 14:21 and 14:31 she is named as the mother of Rehoboam and an Ammonite wife of Solomon, the name appearing in RSV as Naamah the Ammonitess; 1 Kings 14:21 ties her to Rehoboam's reign. The passages show her as a named woman in both the genealogy of early human culture and the royal line of Judah.

senses.definition: An easy or obvious conclusion, decision, solution; something requiring little or no thought.
senses.example: Choosing the older version which was as good as the newer version for half the cost was a no-brainer.

senses.definition: A conundrum requiring little or no thought to solve; A problem with an easy or obvious conclusion, decision, solution.
senses.example: This next exam question is a no-brainer.

core.definition: Something so easy or obvious that it requires almost no thought to decide or solve.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BRAIN, and the final -er is a weak, rhotic syllable, not 'ear'. Learners often pronounce the r too weakly or stress the second word equally.

nuance.connotation: Positive or lighthearted; it signals that a choice is clearly good. It can sound dismissive if the problem is actually complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it casually about decisions that are obviously right, such as 'Free parking? No-brainer.' It is common at work and with friends, but avoid it in formal writing or when a serious issue is at stake. Use 'a no-brainer' with the article when it is a noun.

distinctions.note: A toss-up is a choice where both options are equally good, while a no-brainer has one clearly better option.
Slam dunk is also informal and means a sure success, often used about plans or outcomes rather than simple decisions.

examples.everyday: Free upgrade to the bigger pizza for the same price? That's a no-brainer.
examples.professional: Moving the nightly jobs to the new cluster is a no-brainer, so let's approve it in today's meeting.
examples.analytical: Some dilemmas are really no-brainers, and the effort spent debating them reveals how we value speed over clarity.

nuance.analogy: Like a green light at an empty intersection: the right move is obvious at a glance.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words in formal contexts; the hyphenated form is standard.
Using it for hard problems, which sounds sarcastic or naive to Americans.

conversation.text: Free upgrade to first class? That's a no brainer.
Automating that report is a no-brainer; it saves us hours.
Taking the job closer to home was a no brainer.

senses.definition: A bittersweet yearning for the things of the past.
senses.example: an alumnus' feelings of nostalgia for his/her years in high school

senses.definition: A longing for home or familiar surroundings; homesickness.
senses.example: Seeing food at camp similar to his mother's cooking sent a wave of nostalgia through him.

core.definition: A warm but sad feeling of longing for a past time, place, or person that you remember fondly.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the second syllable, STAL, and the first and last syllables are reduced to schwa. The given IPA put stress on the first syllable, which is incorrect for American speech.

nuance.connotation: mixed; it is bittersweet, usually with a warm sense of longing and sometimes a hint of sadness or idealizing the past.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nostalgia' in everyday conversation about childhood, old songs, favorite TV shows, or hometowns. It is not usually negative, but saying someone is 'stuck in nostalgia' can sound critical. A natural reply to a fond memory is 'Oh, I miss those days too.'

distinctions.note: Homesickness is a more specific feeling of missing your home or family while away, while nostalgia can be about any past time.
Sentimentality is an excessive or overly emotional display of feeling, which can be a criticism, while nostalgia is a more neutral, reflective longing.

examples.everyday: Hearing that old Springsteen song always gives me a little nostalgia for high school.
examples.professional: Our product team's nostalgia for the old interface is making it hard to approve the redesign, even though usage data says otherwise.
examples.analytical: Svetlana Boym distinguishes restorative nostalgia, which seeks to rebuild the lost home, from reflective nostalgia, which dwells on the longing itself.

nuance.analogy: Nostalgia is like looking at an old photograph: it brings back warmth, but you can't step back into the scene.
nuance.etymology: Coined in 1688 by Johannes Hofer from Greek nostos (return home) and algos (pain).
common_mistakes: Putting stress on the first syllable, as in 'NO-stal-gia.'
Using 'nostalgia' for simple memory; it specifically implies an emotional longing for the past.

nostalgia.etymology: From New Latin *nostalgia*, from Ancient Greek *νόστος* (“returning home”) + *ἄλγος* (“pain”), calquing German *Heimweh*.

senses.definition: Of an age suitable for marriage; marriageable (principally of a young woman).
Sexually attractive (especially of a young woman).
A woman of marriageable age; a sexually attractive young woman.

core.definition: Of an age considered suitable for marriage, and usually used to describe a young woman in an attractive way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the last syllable as 'eel' or 'ile' depending on speaker. Americans usually pronounce it with a clear 'bile' sound at the end, and the word has no separate 'ni' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative or objectifying in modern use. It can sound old-fashioned and sexualizing, so it is best avoided in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use nubile today outside of literature, historical writing, or critical discussion of old texts. When used in modern speech, it often sounds objectifying toward young women, so most people choose more neutral words. If you encounter it in a novel, understand it as a formal, somewhat dated way of describing youthful, marriageable women.

distinctions.note: Marriageable is a plainer, more neutral term for being of age to marry, while nubile adds a sexual suggestion.
Attractive is a general, everyday word, while nubile is a literary or old-fashioned way of describing youthful desirability.

examples.everyday: That word 'nubile' sounds like something from an old novel, so I wouldn't use it at a party.
examples.professional: The editor flagged the word nubile in the manuscript as dated and inappropriate for a modern audience.
examples.analytical: The poem's depiction of the nubile bride reveals how the culture tied female worth to marriageability.

nuance.analogy: Nubile is like an antique label: it tells you what people once valued, but it sounds strange on modern products.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nubilis, 'marriageable,' from nubere, 'to marry.'
common_mistakes: Using nubile as a neutral synonym for 'young' in modern conversation, which can sound objectifying or old-fashioned.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'nu-BILE'.

nubile.etymology: From French *nubile*, from Latin *nūbilis* (“marriageable”), from *nūbō* (“marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European **snewbʰ-* (“to marry, to wed”).

senses.definition: Demonstration of an obedient attitude, especially by bowing deeply; a deep bow which demonstrates such an attitude.
An obedient attitude.

core.definition: A deep bow or gesture showing respect, submission, or humble obedience toward someone of higher rank or authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BAY. Don't pronounce the first syllable as 'oh-bee'; the ei is a long a sound, and the final -ance is a reduced 'uns'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: it describes submission or servility, and it can suggest someone is being too humble or subservient.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in historical, literary, or journalistic writing about court ceremonies, religious worship, or hierarchical settings. You will rarely hear it in casual speech. In everyday life, say 'bow' or 'show respect' instead.

distinctions.note: Respect is a general attitude of esteem; obeisance is the outward act of bowing or submitting, often to someone in power.
Homage is praise or honor paid publicly, often admiringly; obeisance stresses bodily submission or deference.

examples.everyday: At the wedding, the old man made a little obeisance to the bride's grandmother, and everyone laughed at how formal he was.
examples.professional: In the historical novel I'm editing, the messenger enters the throne room and performs obeisance before the king.
examples.analytical: Medieval court ritual often reduced political hierarchy to the body, so that obeisance became a visible sign of the subject's submission to the crown.

nuance.analogy: Obeisance is like a bow in a theater curtain call, but the bow is owed to a king instead of an audience.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French obeisance, from obeir, 'to obey'.
common_mistakes: Using obeisance as a verb; the verb is 'make obeisance' or 'do obeisance'.
Pronouncing it with the stress on the first syllable, as in 'OH-bee-sence'.

obeisance.etymology: From Middle English *obeisaunce* (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French *obeissance*, derived from *obeissant* (“obedient”), participle of *obeir* (“to obey”), from Latin *oboediō*, *obēdiō*; *ob-* (“to, for”) + *audiō* (“to hear”).

senses.definition: The state of being obsolete—no longer in use; gone into disuse; disused or neglected.
The process of becoming obsolete, outmoded or out of date.

core.definition: The process by which something, such as a product or skill, becomes outdated and no longer useful or in use.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress is on LES, the third syllable. The first syllable is 'AHB', with the 'ob' sound in the cot vowel. Stress the final syllable lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, often describing progress or economic change, but can carry a sense of loss when applied to skills or people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'obsolescence' mainly in business, technology, and engineering, as in 'planned obsolescence,' a term for designing products to wear out sooner. In everyday talk, people more often say 'out of date' or 'becoming outdated.' The word sounds formal and somewhat technical in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Outdated is a common, everyday word, while obsolescence names the process or state in a formal way.
Deprecation in software means a feature is discouraged but still works; obsolescence means it is no longer used or supported at all.

examples.everyday: My phone is slow, and I think it's approaching obsolescence, so I'm thinking about upgrading.
examples.professional: We need to plan for hardware obsolescence before the next budget cycle, or we'll be stuck on old servers.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that planned obsolescence is less about technology and more about sustaining consumer demand.

nuance.analogy: Obsolescence is like a map that stays folded in the glovebox long after the highway it shows has been rebuilt.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obsolescere, to fall into disuse, from obsolescere, to grow old.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'ob-so-LES-cence' with a weak 'so' that becomes 'suh'.
Using 'obsolescence' as a verb; the verb is 'become obsolete' or 'obsolesce'.

senses.definition: Allowing movement, vision, etc. in only one direction; unidirectional.
senses.example: one-way mirror

senses.definition: Allowing travel in only one direction.
senses.example: I bought a one-way ticket to Leeds.

senses.definition: Of a function: easy to compute for every input, but hard to invert given the image of a random input.
To use a disc harrow to turn the soil and kill weeds, in preparation for planting seeds.
A one-way trip or flight.

core.definition: Allowing movement, travel, or traffic in only one direction, such as a one-way street or a one-way ticket.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WUN, and say 'one' as 'wun', not 'won' or 'oh-nee'. The second word 'way' has a clear long 'ay' vowel and is not stressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, practical, and direct.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'one-way ticket' for a flight or bus ride that does not include a return trip, and 'one-way street' for traffic. In the United States 'single' is mostly used in British contexts, so 'one-way' is the normal word. You might hear 'one-way rental' when renting a car to drop it off in another city.

distinctions.note: A two-way street or two-way radio allows movement or communication in both directions.
A round-trip ticket covers the journey there and back, while a one-way ticket covers only one direction.

examples.everyday: I'm flying home, so I'll book a one-way ticket and figure out the return later.
examples.professional: We'll make the connection one-way, so the service can push updates but not receive them.
examples.analytical: A one-way function is easy to compute but practically hard to invert, which is the basis of many cryptographic schemes.

nuance.analogy: Like a revolving door that only turns one way.
nuance.etymology: From 'one' plus 'way', from Old English weg.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'way' as in wun-WAY, which sounds unnatural
Saying 'single ticket', which is mainly British and sounds unusual to Americans

conversation.text: I bought a one-way ticket because I don't know when I'm coming back.
You can't turn there; it's a one-way street.
The rental is one-way, so I'm dropping it off in Denver.

senses.definition: The practice of taking advantage of any situations or people to achieve an end, often with no regard for principles or consequences.

The political line of Communist Party members who zealously support the Party, but whose trait is that they yield to the mood of the moment, they are unable to resist what is fashionable, leading to the sacrifice of the permanent and essential interests of the Party to the momentary and minor interests.

core.definition: The habit of taking advantage of any situation for personal gain, often without regard for principles or long-term consequences.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'too,' with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. Keep the middle syllables reduced, so the word sounds like 'ah-per-TOO-nih-zum.'

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'opportunism' in news, business, and politics to describe people who change their positions to gain advantage. It is a strong criticism, so saying it about a colleague or politician can sound harsh. In casual conversation, people often say 'they're just looking out for themselves' instead.

distinctions.note: Pragmatism means practical decision-making based on what works, while opportunism implies a lack of principle in pursuing personal advantage.
Ambition is a desire to achieve something, and it is neutral or positive, while opportunism is negative because it involves taking advantage of others.

examples.everyday: My neighbor thinks the company's new discount is pure opportunism, since they raised prices last month.
examples.professional: Leadership was criticized for opportunism when it dropped the project after the competitor launched a similar product.
examples.analytical: Hobbes's account of self-interest tends to explain opportunism as a rational response to a situation with no enforceable rules.

nuance.analogy: Opportunism is like a sailor who changes course to follow whatever wind is blowing, with no fixed destination.
nuance.etymology: From 'opportunist' with the suffix -ism, from Latin opportunus, 'favorable' or 'convenient.'
common_mistakes: Using 'opportunism' as a neutral word, when it usually has a negative tone.
Confusing it with 'opportunity,' which describes a favorable chance rather than the behavior of taking advantage.

senses.definition: Someone who takes advantage of any opportunity to advance their own situation, placing expediency above principle.

core.definition: A person who takes advantage of any chance to benefit, often at the expense of principles or other people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'too,' and the 'r' in 'per' is clear in American speech. The 'tj' sound in the British version is not used in General American, so it is simply 'too.'

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'opportunist' for someone who takes advantage of changing circumstances for selfish reasons. It is often used in news, politics, and workplace criticism. It can sound harsh, so use it carefully when talking about someone you know.

distinctions.note: A schemer plans secretly and carefully, while an opportunist reacts quickly to chances as they appear.
A careerist focuses on advancement, which may be honest or ambitious, while an opportunist may ignore principles to gain an advantage.

examples.everyday: My brother says the new salesman is an opportunist, because he only started calling me after I got a promotion.
examples.professional: Our manager warned the team not to become opportunists who chase every new trend without a plan.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli's prince can appear as an opportunist, but his strategy depends on reading circumstances with discipline.

nuance.analogy: An opportunist is like a surfer who waits for the biggest wave and rides it wherever it goes, with no fixed direction.
nuance.etymology: From French opportuniste, from Latin opportunus, 'favorable' or 'convenient.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables as a full 'tyoon,' rather than the American 'too' sound.
Using it as a neutral word, when it usually carries a negative judgment.

senses.definition: The reduction of a program or algorithm to its most efficient form, as during compilation, by removing unused portions of code and improving the speed or resource usage of others.
The design and operation of a system or process to make it as good as possible in some defined sense.

core.definition: The process of making a system, design, or program as efficient or effective as possible.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'ZAY,' and the ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun.' Keep the 'ay' in 'my' and 'zay' as full diphthongs.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes improvement, though it can sound jargon-heavy in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'optimization' mainly in mathematics, engineering, data science, and business. In software it often means making code or queries run faster. In everyday talk, people more often say 'making things more efficient.'

distinctions.note: 'Improvement' is general; 'optimization' implies a systematic search for the best possible configuration.
'Efficiency' is a quality or measure; 'optimization' is the process of achieving it.

examples.everyday: My phone's battery life got better after I turned on some optimization settings.
examples.professional: Our next sprint focuses on query optimization, since the dashboard loads too slowly for users.
examples.analytical: Optimization theory assumes that the objective function is well defined, and that assumption is often what is quietly contested in ethics.

nuance.analogy: Like tuning an engine until it gets the most power from each gallon of fuel.
nuance.etymology: From 'optimize,' from Latin optimus, 'best,' with the suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the '-ation' ending as 'ay-shun' with an extra syllable, or stressing 'op-TIM' incorrectly.
Using 'optimization' for any kind of improvement; it usually implies a measurable best result.

senses.definition: To disperse too much or too far.
To produce overdispersion.

core.definition: In statistics, to have more variability in counts or values than a given model predicts, so the spread exceeds what the model allows.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable of 'disperse,' and 'over' keeps a lighter secondary stress. Use a short i in the middle syllable and clearly pronounce the final -st.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term that describes data spread without judging the data or the analyst.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this almost only in statistics, epidemiology, ecology and data science, especially in reports about count data such as crashes, infections or word frequencies. You will hear it in technical meetings and read it in papers, not in casual talk. Calling a dataset overdispersed signals that a simple model, such as a Poisson model, may be inadequate.

distinctions.note: Dispersed simply means spread out, while overdispersed means spread more widely than a specified model predicts.
Underdispersed is the opposite condition, where the data vary less than the model expects, and it is much less common in practice.

collocations: test whether the data are overdispersed

examples.everyday: My friend who runs a wildlife lab said the bird counts looked overdispersed, and I had no idea what she meant.
examples.professional: The Poisson fit looks poor because the crash counts are overdispersed, so let's try a negative binomial model.
examples.analytical: When the residual variance substantially exceeds the mean, the count data are overdispersed relative to the Poisson assumption.

nuance.analogy: Like a shotgun pattern that scatters wider than the gun's design says it should.
nuance.etymology: From over- (excessive) plus disperse, from Latin dispergere, 'to scatter apart.'
common_mistakes: Treating overdispersed as a general word for 'spread out'; in statistics it is measured against a specific model's expected variance.
Thinking overdispersion means the data are wrong or corrupted; it only means the variance is larger than the model assumed.

senses.definition: Sorrow; grief; mourning or sadness.

core.definition: In Orthodox spirituality, a holy sorrow or grief over sin that softens the heart and leads to repentance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the 'th' as in 'think', then end with an 'ahs' sound, not 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in spiritual contexts, where it describes grief that leads to healing. It can sound obscure outside theological or monastic writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use penthos mainly in Orthodox theology, monastic writing and academic study of spirituality. In ordinary speech, people say grief, mourning or sorrow for sins. The word comes from Greek, so it appears most often in books, retreats and sermons that draw on Eastern Christian traditions.

distinctions.note: Compunction is the sense of guilt or regret that pricks the conscience, while penthos is a deeper, grace-filled grief that continues in prayer.
Grief in everyday English is usually loss, while penthos in Orthodox use is sorrow for sin and separation from God.

examples.everyday: My friend used the word penthos in our Bible study to describe grief over sin, not just ordinary sadness.
examples.professional: In the retreat talk, the priest described penthos as a gift that softens the heart before God.
examples.analytical: Ascetic writers treat penthos not as a passing emotion but as a stage of spiritual purification that leads to prayer.

nuance.analogy: Penthos is like the sorrow of a child who sees how much a parent has been hurt, and wants to make things right with love rather than fear.
nuance.etymology: From Greek penthos, meaning grief, sorrow or mourning.
common_mistakes: Using penthos as a general word for sadness in everyday English.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pen-THOS', when the first syllable is strong.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb penthein (to mourn) appears in Matthew 5:4, where the RSV reads 'Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.' Luke 6:25 warns those who laugh now that they will mourn and weep. Romans 12:15 calls believers to weep with those who weep. These passages connect grief with the blessing of God's comfort.

traditions.view: Penthos is a recognized gift of holy mourning, developed by desert fathers and ascetic writers, which leads to tears of repentance and prayer.
Catholic spirituality speaks of contrition and compunction, which describe similar sorrow for sin, but penthos is not usually a named category in Catholic teaching.
Protestants describe sorrow for sin as conviction and repentance, and the term penthos is rarely used in Protestant theology.

senses.definition: To become more lively or enthusiastic.
To become more upright.
senses.example: His ears perked up when he heard there would be ice cream.

senses.definition: To cause to be more lively or enthusiastic.
To cause to be more upright, straighten up.

core.definition: To suddenly become more lively, interested or cheerful, often after feeling tired or bored.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'up' gets the main stress. Say 'perk' lightly and link the words so it sounds like 'per-kup', with the final 'p' of 'up' often barely released.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a happy change in energy or mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perk up constantly in casual speech, about people, pets, or even the weather. It is usually used intransitively, as in 'she perked up.' The transitive form 'perk someone up' is also common, as in 'a cup of coffee perked me up.'

distinctions.note: Cheer up is used when someone who is sad or upset begins to feel better. Perk up describes a quick increase in energy or interest, even without sadness.
Wake up means to stop sleeping. Perk up means to become more alert or lively while already awake.

examples.everyday: When I mentioned pizza, the kids perked up right away.
examples.professional: The team perked up when the client approved the new budget.
examples.analytical: Once the evidence was presented, the skeptical audience perked up and began to weigh the argument seriously.

nuance.analogy: Perk up is like a plant that was drooping in the heat and stands up straight after a little water.
nuance.etymology: 'Perk' meaning brisk or jaunty comes from Middle English; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on 'perk' when the particle carries the main stress.
Using 'perk up' as a separable verb with the wrong word order, such as 'perk up it' instead of 'perk it up'.

conversation.text: He perked up as soon as he heard about the pizza.
A cup of coffee always perks me up.
Sales usually perk up around the holidays.

senses.definition: A list of recorded songs scheduled to be played on a radio station.
A list of tracks or videos to be played in a particular sequence, as from an audio CD or a streaming service.
A list of songs, prepared for a band or musical artist, to be performed during a concert; a setlist.
To include (a track) on a playlist.
senses.example: She achieved success when her first single was playlisted on national radio.

core.definition: A list of songs or videos set to play in a particular order, often on a streaming service or device.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PLAY, and the second syllable is short and unstressed, so 'list' sounds like 'lihst.' Don't stress the second word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday. It can sound casual in a professional setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use playlist daily for streaming services like Spotify and Apple Music. You can make one, share one, or 'add it to my playlist.' In a music context, a setlist is the list of songs a live band plays in concert.

distinctions.note: A playlist is for recorded music played in order; a setlist is the songs a band plans to perform live.
An album is a set of songs released together by an artist; a playlist can mix songs from many artists.

collocations: add a song to a playlist

examples.everyday: I made a workout playlist, so you can borrow it when we go running.
examples.professional: I'll add the new onboarding videos to the training playlist so everyone can watch them in order.
examples.analytical: Streaming platforms use algorithmic playlists to shape listeners' tastes, which raises questions about curation and authorship.

nuance.analogy: A playlist is like a recipe card for a mood: you pick the ingredients and the order they come in.
nuance.etymology: From play plus list; the sense 'list of recordings' dates from the late twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'play-LIST.'
Using playlist for a concert song order, where setlist is the natural word.

conversation.text: Can you make a playlist for the road trip?
I have a workout playlist that keeps me going.
Send me the playlist from the party!

senses.definition: The state of being practical or feasible.
The practical aspect of something.

core.definition: The quality of being workable, realistic, or useful in actual situations, rather than only in theory.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress moves from the first syllable of practical to the third syllable, KAL, in practicality. The final -ity is pronounced ih-tee, with the vowel reduced.

nuance.connotation: positive. It usually praises realism or efficiency, though it can sound dry when used to dismiss ideals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use practicality in business, engineering, and design discussions, such as 'the practicality of the plan.' The plural practicalities means the everyday logistics of doing something, as in 'Let's talk about the practicalities.' In casual talk, people often say 'how practical is it' rather than using the noun.

distinctions.note: Practicality is the abstract quality, while practicalities is the plural noun for specific logistical details.
Feasibility is a more formal, technical term for whether something can be done, while practicality also includes usefulness and convenience.

examples.everyday: I love the idea of a backyard garden, but I'm not sure about the practicality of it in this heat.
examples.professional: Before we commit, we need to test the practicality of the new workflow with the support team.
examples.analytical: The author questions the practicality of such a moral system, asking whether it can survive contact with ordinary life.

nuance.analogy: Like a sturdy hand tool, judged by whether it works in your hands on a real job.
nuance.etymology: From practical with the suffix -ity; practical comes from Late Latin practicalis, from Greek praktikos, meaning active.
common_mistakes: Using practicality for a single detail; the plural practicalities is used for specific issues.
Placing the stress on the first syllable as in practical, rather than on KAL.

senses.definition: An enclosed space having defined limits, normally marked by walls.
The general area surrounding a place, environs.
A subdivision of a city or other locality for the purposes of voting and representation in local government. In cities, precincts may be grouped into wards.
A subdivision of a city under the jurisdiction of a specific group of police; the police station situated in that district.

core.definition: A defined district of a city or county, used for police patrol or for voting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, PREE. The 'ct' at the end is a single 'kt' cluster, so do not insert a vowel between the 'ng' and the 'k'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in police contexts it can sound official or tense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use precinct for a police station and its district, as in 'the 15th Precinct', and for a voting district, as in 'Which precinct are you in?'. The older sense of an enclosed courtyard or grounds appears mainly in historic or literary writing. In British English, a precinct can also be a shopping area, where Americans would say shopping center or mall.

distinctions.note: A district is a broad administrative area, while a precinct is a smaller subdivision often used for voting or policing.
A ward is a city division for electing council members, and several precincts can make up one ward.

examples.everyday: I have to vote at the elementary school because that's our precinct.
examples.professional: The county released turnout numbers by precinct, so we can compare trends across districts.
examples.analytical: The medieval precinct of the cathedral was a space legally set apart from the surrounding town.

nuance.analogy: A precinct is like one slice of a pizza: the city is the whole pie, and each precinct is one clearly defined slice.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin praecinctum, 'enclosed area', from Latin praecingere, 'to surround'.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'precint', with a missing 'c'.
Using precinct for a shopping mall; Americans say shopping center or mall.

precinct.etymology: From Middle English *precinct*, early 15th century, in sense of “district for government purposes”, from Medieval Latin *precinctum*, alternative form of *praecinctum* (“enclosure, boundary line”), neuter singular of *praecinctus*, perfect passive…

senses.definition: In a premature manner; too soon or too early.
senses.example: publish an obituary prematurely

core.definition: Too soon or too early; before the expected or proper time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, -TUR-, with a light secondary stress on pree-. Say the r in -tur- clearly, and reduce the middle vowel to a quick uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context. It often suggests a bad result, such as a baby born too early or a decision made before the facts were in.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prematurely mostly in news, medicine, business and serious conversation. In casual talk people often say too early or too soon instead. It is a common, natural word in both writing and speech.

distinctions.note: Early is neutral and can describe a good thing, as in arriving early. Prematurely implies that the timing was a mistake or caused harm.
Too soon is conversational and direct. Prematurely is more formal and suggests a judgment about a poor outcome.

examples.everyday: Don't celebrate yet, we might be getting our hopes up prematurely.
examples.professional: We should not announce the launch date prematurely, since legal has not signed off yet.
examples.analytical: A theory that claims to explain the whole system from a few data points is prematurely confident.

nuance.analogy: Like picking an apple before it ripens: the fruit is there, but it is not ready.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praematurus, meaning too early, from prae (before) and maturus (ripe).
common_mistakes: Saying prematurily with an extra i; the correct spelling is prematurely.
Stressing the first syllable, as in PRE-mature-ly; the stress belongs on -TUR-.

senses.definition: In AI: Already trained on a large general dataset, ready to be fine-tuned or used directly.
Having been trained before.
Having undergone initial training to acquire a base of general-purpose knowledge, representations, or capabilities.

core.definition: In AI, already trained on a large general dataset so it can be fine-tuned for a specific task or used directly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PREE, the first syllable. The 'pre' is a long 'ee' sound, and the final 'ed' is pronounced as a 'd', not as 'ed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a positive description of a model that saves time and data.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pretrained mostly in data science, machine learning, and AI conversations. It usually comes before the noun, as in 'a pretrained model,' or after a verb, as in 'the model was pretrained on web text.' When explaining to a client, you can say 'a model that already learned from a huge general dataset.' Many writers also use the spelling 'pre-trained'.

distinctions.note: A pretrained model is trained first on general data; fine-tuning is the further training that adapts it to a specific task.
A model trained from scratch starts with random weights; a pretrained model starts with knowledge learned from a broad dataset.
Untrained means no learning has happened yet; pretrained means general learning has already been done.

examples.everyday: My kid's new drawing app uses a pretrained model, so it recognizes cats without any setup.
examples.professional: We can start with a pretrained model and fine-tune it on our claims data instead of training from scratch.
examples.analytical: A pretrained representation transfers statistical structure from a broad corpus to narrower tasks, which is why it generalizes with fewer labels.

nuance.analogy: Like a new employee who already knows the basics of the industry, so training focuses only on the company's specific work.
nuance.etymology: From pre- ('before') and trained, from Old French trainer, 'to drag or draw along'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'pre-TRAYND' instead of 'PREE-traynd'.
Pronouncing the final 'ed' as an extra syllable, 'PREE-tray-ned'.

conversation.text: We started from pretrained weights rather than random initialization, which cut training time dramatically.
The model was pretrained on a mix of web text, books, and code before any fine-tuning.
Pretrained means the model already learned general language patterns before we taught it your specific task.

senses.definition: A person who is guided and supported by an older and more experienced person (a protector or mentor).
senses.example: His status as a protégé of the great artist had many benefits, but was ultimately a burden.

core.definition: A person, usually younger or less experienced, who is guided, trained and supported by a more senior mentor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the final syllable like the French-derived zh sound followed by ay. Drop the French accent in speech and do not pronounce a final t.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests respect, growth and a good mentoring relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protégé in workplaces, universities and professional circles, often when someone says a colleague is their protégé. For a woman, protégée is the traditional feminine form, though many people now use protégé for everyone. In casual talk people often say mentee, which is more common in corporate settings.

distinctions.note: Mentee is the common modern workplace term, while protégé sounds more classic and suggests a close relationship of support and influence.
An apprentice learns a trade formally, often through a set training period, while a protégé is supported more broadly by a patron.

examples.everyday: My aunt is a famous chef, and she's been like a mentor to her protégé, a young cook from her restaurant.
examples.professional: Our VP of engineering has been championing her protégé for the lead role on the data platform team.
examples.analytical: The relationship between a master and protégé shapes not only skill but also the moral style that a student inherits.

nuance.analogy: A protégé is like a plant grown in a greenhouse: carefully supported until it is strong enough to stand on its own.
nuance.etymology: From French protégé, past participle of protéger, to protect, from Latin protegere.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word as PRO-tee-gay, with a long e in the middle.
Forgetting the accent mark on the final e in written English, which is usually kept in formal writing.

senses.definition: In AI: Removing weights or neurons that contribute little, to make a model smaller and faster.
A removal of excess material from a tree or shrub.
A method of enumeration that allows the cutting out of parts of a decision tree.
Something obtained by pruning, as a twig.

core.definition: In AI, removing weights or neurons that contribute little, so a trained neural network becomes smaller and faster.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PROO. The second syllable is short and unstressed, so do not stretch it into 'PROO-neeng'. The -ing ending is a short ih sound plus ng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In gardening it is a positive, healthy activity; in AI it is a neutral engineering step with no negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American machine learning and data science teams, pruning is a standard term in papers, code, and meetings about model compression. Engineers often say they pruned the model to mean they cut its size. Outside tech, Americans use it about gardening, so the meaning depends on context.

distinctions.note: Pruning removes weights or neurons, while quantization lowers the numerical precision of the weights; teams often use both.
Distillation trains a smaller model to copy a larger one, while pruning shrinks the existing model by removing parts.

examples.everyday: My gardener is pruning the roses this weekend, so the bushes should look better in spring.
examples.professional: After pruning the network, we cut the model size by forty percent and the inference latency dropped noticeably.
examples.analytical: Pruning raises a question about which parameters carry the model's function, since removing low-magnitude weights can preserve accuracy while revealing redundancy in the learned representation.

nuance.analogy: Pruning a neural network is like trimming a hedge: you cut the branches that add little, so the plant stays healthy and easier to manage.
nuance.etymology: Derived from the verb prune, meaning to trim branches.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stressed vowel as a long i, as in 'PRY-ning'.
Using pruning to mean deleting data; in AI it refers to removing parts of a model.

conversation.text: Pruning removes weights or whole neurons that contribute little, making the model smaller.
Unstructured pruning often saves less in practice than expected, because sparse matrices are hard to accelerate.
Spring pruning keeps the rose bushes healthy.

senses.definition: Having a tendency to argue or fight; aggressive, combative.

core.definition: Quick to argue or fight; aggressive, combative and eager to start a conflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the NAY syllable, the second syllable of the word. The first vowel is the short uh of cup, and the ending is shus, not shee-us.

nuance.connotation: negative; it describes someone who is too eager to fight or argue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pugnacious in news, sports coverage and descriptions of people who are combative, often in politics or online debate. It is more formal than mad or angry and can sound slightly literary. It describes a personality trait rather than a single outburst.

distinctions.note: Aggressive can describe behavior in general, including business or sports, while pugnacious focuses on a fighting or quarrelsome temperament.
Belligerent is stronger and often implies open hostility or a readiness to make war, while pugnacious suggests a tendency to argue or fight over small things.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor gets pretty pugnacious whenever someone parks in his spot.
examples.professional: Keep the feedback constructive, because the pugnacious tone in that thread will discourage people from speaking up.
examples.analytical: The pugnacious style of the polemicist may win applause, but it rarely persuades the undecided reader.

nuance.analogy: A pugnacious person is like a dog that barks at every passing car, always ready to start a fight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pugnax, combative, from pugnare, to fight.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable, as in PUG-nay-shus.
Confusing pugnacious with pugilistic, which is more often used for boxing.

senses.definition: An instance of the action of a pump; one stroke of a pump; any action similar to pumping.
senses.example: It takes thirty pumps to get 10 liters; he did 50 pumps of the weights.

senses.definition: A device for dispensing liquid or gas to be sold, particularly fuel; a gas pump.
senses.example: This pump is out of order, but you can gas up at the next one.

senses.definition: A device for moving or compressing a liquid or gas.
senses.example: This pump can deliver 100 gallons of water per minute.

senses.definition: A swelling of the muscles caused by increased blood flow following high intensity weightlifting.
A ride on a bicycle given to a passenger, usually on the handlebars or fender.
senses.example: She gave the other girl a pump on her new bike.

senses.definition: The heart.
A type of women's shoe which leaves the instep uncovered and has a relatively high heel, especially a stiletto (with a very high and thin heel)
senses.example: She was wearing a lovely new pair of pumps.

senses.definition: A dancing shoe.
A type of shoe without a heel.(Can we add an example for this sense?)
To use a pump; to move (water or other liquid) by means of a pump.
senses.example: I've been pumping for over a minute but the water isn't coming through.

senses.definition: To inject or pour (something) into someone or something in a manner similar to a pump.
To express milk from (a breast) by means of a breast pump.
To fill with air by means of a pump; to inflate.
senses.example: He pumped up the air-bed by hand, but used the service station air to pump up the tires.

senses.definition: To move rhythmically, as the motion of a pump.
senses.example: I pumped my fist with joy when I won the race.

senses.definition: To load a shell into the chamber of a pump-action shotgun by pumping the mechanism.
senses.example: He ran on, pumping another round up into his scattergun.

senses.definition: To gain something, especially information, from (a person) by persistent questioning.
To enlarge the body by means of weightlifting or steroid use.
To shake (a person's hand) vigorously.
Of music: to be loud, to have strong bass and rhythms; to be full of energy.
senses.example: The waves were really pumping this morning.

senses.definition: To pass (messages) into a program so that it can obey them.
To inject silicone into the body in order to try to achieve a fuller or curvier look.
To fire a bullet from a firearm.
To kick, throw, or hit the ball far and high.

core.definition: The machine at a gas station from which you pump fuel into your car; the dispenser you use to fill your tank.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short u sound of cup, not the oo of pool. End with a clean mp cluster without adding a vowel after the p.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical, used in everyday driving life.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, people say pump for the fuel dispenser and gas station for the place. Phrases such as 'pump number four' or 'I'll pay at the pump' are very common, and pump gas or pumping gas is a casual way to say fill up the tank. Britons would say petrol station and forecourt, so American usage differs here.

distinctions.note: A pump is the machine that dispenses fuel, while a gas station is the entire business with its store and lot.
Gas is the fuel itself in everyday American speech, while pump is the machine; pump gas is an informal way to refer to fueling.
Pumps in the plural can mean women's shoes, which is an unrelated sense of the same word.

examples.everyday: I'll grab a coffee while you fill up at the next pump.
examples.professional: The fleet card works at any pump, so drivers do not need to pay inside at the register.
examples.analytical: Economists studying fuel prices often track the posted price at the pump, since it shapes consumer expectations.

nuance.analogy: Like a straw that draws the drink from the glass into your mouth.
common_mistakes: Using gas station to mean the pump itself
Saying pumping the gas in formal writing when pump gas or fill the tank is more natural

pump.etymology: From Middle English *pumpe*, possibly from Middle Dutch *pompe* (“pipe, water conduit”) or *pumpe* (“pump”), probably ultimately.

conversation.text: Pump number four isn't working, so pull up to the next one.
In New Jersey, you aren't allowed to pump your own gas.
I need to pump up my tires; the warning light came on.

senses.definition: A polygon with four sides.
An area defended by four fortresses supporting each other.
senses.example: The Venetian quadrilateral comprised Mantua, Peschiera, Verona, and Legnano.

senses.definition: Having four sides.
senses.example: They spoke at a quadrilateral meeting of the trade ministers of the United States, the European Union, Canada, and Japan.

core.definition: A flat shape or polygon with exactly four straight sides, such as a square, rectangle, or trapezoid.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on LAT, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, and the t in 'lateral' is a flap, so it sounds close to a d.

nuance.connotation: neutral and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: In American schools, quadrilateral is the standard word for any four-sided polygon, and students learn it in geometry. Everyday speakers usually say 'four-sided shape' or name the specific shape, such as square or rectangle. The word is used in the military sense of a fortified area only in historical writing.

distinctions.note: A square is one specific quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles; quadrilateral covers all four-sided polygons.
A polygon is any closed shape with straight sides; quadrilateral is the subset with exactly four sides.

collocations: sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral

examples.everyday: The tile pattern in the kitchen is a quadrilateral shape, so the pieces fit together easily.
examples.professional: The design team needs the plot to be a quadrilateral, so the survey points define four boundary corners.
examples.analytical: Any simple quadrilateral has interior angles that sum to 360 degrees, which follows from splitting it into two triangles.

nuance.analogy: A quadrilateral is a four-cornered fence around a yard, no matter how crooked the sides are.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quadrilaterus, from quadri- 'four' and latus 'side'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying kwah-drih-LAT-er-al with a full vowel in the last syllable.
Using quadrilateral for a shape with more than four sides.

senses.definition: To satisfy, especially a literal or figurative thirst.
senses.example: The library quenched her thirst for knowledge.

senses.definition: To extinguish or put out (as a fire or light).
To cool rapidly by direct contact with liquid coolant, as a blacksmith quenching hot iron.
senses.example: The swordsmith quenched the sword in an oil bath so that it wouldn't shatter.

senses.definition: To terminate or greatly diminish (a chemical reaction) by destroying or deforming the remaining reagents.
To rapidly change the parameters of a physical system.
To rapidly terminate the operation of a superconducting electromagnet by causing part or all of the magnet's windings to enter the normal, resistive state.
senses.example: If someone is pinned against the MRI magnet by a ferromagnetic object, you may need to quench the magnet in order to free them.

senses.definition: The act of quenching something; the fact of being quenched.
The abnormal termination of operation of a superconducting magnet, occurring when part of the superconducting coil enters the normal (resistive) state.
A rapid change of the parameters of a physical system.

core.definition: To satisfy a thirst, or to put out a fire or flame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the only syllable, with a short 'e' like 'bench'. End with a clear 'ch' sound, not a 'sh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing thirst relieved; neutral or negative when describing fires or hopes being ended.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'quench' most naturally with thirst, as in 'a cold drink to quench your thirst,' a phrase used in ads and everyday talk. For fires, Americans more often say 'put out' or 'extinguish'. In figurative use, 'quench' appears in writing about hope, enthusiasm or curiosity.

distinctions.note: 'Satisfy' is general for fulfilling any need; 'quench' is specific to thirst or a burning feeling.
'Extinguish' is formal and used for fires or lights; 'quench' is more literary or idiomatic.
'Douse' means to drench or soak something with water; 'quench' focuses on stopping heat or thirst.

examples.everyday: After the hike, a big glass of lemonade really quenched my thirst.
examples.professional: The new budget will quench the team's need for better tools, so we can finally fix the old pipeline.
examples.analytical: The sermon argues that spiritual hunger is not quenched by material success alone.

nuance.analogy: Quench is like pouring water on a campfire: the heat and flame stop when the water reaches them.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'cwencan' (to extinguish, quench), related to 'cwincan' (to vanish).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'qu' as 'k' alone; it is 'kw' with a clear 'w' sound.
Saying 'quench the fire' in casual speech where 'put out the fire' is more common.

quench.etymology: From Middle English *quenchen*, from Old English *cwenċan*, from Proto-Germanic **kwankijaną*.

senses.definition: A thing or person that is genuine, authentic, or worthy of serious regard.
An authentic bargain.
A beneficial result or a favorable state of affairs.

core.definition: Something or someone genuine and authentic, not a fake, imitation, or copy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'deal'. Link the words so it sounds like 'reel-DEEL', and keep the 'r' strongly pronounced at the start.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises authenticity and quality, often with enthusiasm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the real deal' casually about people, food, music, or products they admire, such as 'This pizza is the real deal.' It is informal, so avoid it in formal writing. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it really is' or 'No kidding!'

distinctions.note: 'The genuine article' is similar but slightly more formal and emphasizes true origin rather than general quality.
'The real thing' is very common and can be casual or neutral, while 'the real deal' often carries stronger praise.

examples.everyday: That taco truck on Fifth Street is the real deal, so get the carnitas.
examples.professional: The new engineer is the real deal; she caught the data pipeline bug in under an hour.
examples.analytical: Critics debated whether the memoir was the real deal or a carefully staged performance of honesty.

nuance.analogy: Like a diamond among cubic zirconia, 'the real deal' separates what is authentic from what only looks similar.
nuance.etymology: From 'real' (genuine) and 'deal' in the sense of a transaction or matter, now used idiomatically.
common_mistakes: Using 'real deal' for a bargain in ordinary speech; in American English it usually means authentic.
Writing 'the real deal' without 'the' in the idiomatic sense.

conversation.text: This taco truck is the real deal; it tastes just like Mexico City.
The new hire is the real deal. She knows her stuff.
After one bite, I knew this barbecue was the real deal.

senses.definition: To summarize or repeat in concise form.
senses.example: The entire symphony was recapitulated in the last four bars.

senses.definition: To reproduce or closely resemble (as in structure or function).
To mirror or repeat in analogous form, especially in reference to an individual's development passing through stages corresponding to the species' stages of evolutionary development.

core.definition: To summarize the main points of something in short form, or to repeat them in order.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on PICH, with a secondary stress on the first syllable, REE. The middle -uh- syllables are reduced, and the final -ate is a clear 'ayt'. The 'tch' is one sound, like in 'pitch'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it describes a careful, orderly summary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use recapitulate in academic, legal, and formal writing or speech, for example 'Let me recapitulate the main findings.' In everyday talk they say 'recap' or 'sum up' instead. It can sound stiff at casual gatherings, so reserve it for presentations, papers, or formal settings.

distinctions.note: Recap is the casual, everyday form; recapitulate is more formal and literary.
Summarize is the general word for condensing any content; recapitulate implies repeating the sequence of main points.
Reiterate means saying something again for emphasis; recapitulate means restating the whole structure briefly.

examples.everyday: My uncle likes to recapitulate the whole trip before we leave, just to make sure nothing was forgotten.
examples.professional: Before we open questions, I'll recapitulate the three findings from the pilot and the risks we identified.
examples.analytical: The conclusion recapitulates the argument of the first chapter, showing how each premise leads to the final claim.

nuance.analogy: To recapitulate is like replaying the highlight reel of a game: the key plays come back quickly in the same order.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin recapitulare, 'to sum up', from re- plus capitulum, 'chapter, heading'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the wrong syllable, such as ree-kuh-PIT-yoo-layt; the stress is on PICH.
Using recapitulate for simply repeating a point; it implies summarizing the whole sequence.

recapitulate.etymology: From Late Latin *recapitulātus*, past participle of *recapitulāre* (“to go over the main points of a thing again”), from *re-* + *capitulum*, from *caput* + *ulus*; see *capitulate*.

senses.definition: Careless or heedless; headstrong or rash.
Indifferent or oblivious to danger or the consequences thereof.

core.definition: Doing dangerous or foolish things without thinking about the consequences or the risk to yourself or others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, REK, and the final syllable is a reduced 'lus'. Americans often reduce the middle vowel, so it sounds like 'REK-lus' with no strong vowel in the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes someone for taking unnecessary risks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reckless about drivers, spending, or decisions that risk harm, such as 'reckless driving' or 'reckless behavior'. It is a strong word, so it can sound harsh about a friend. A softer alternative is 'careless' or 'impulsive'.

distinctions.note: Careless means not paying enough attention, while reckless means ignoring obvious danger on purpose.
Bold is often positive and courageous, while reckless suggests a harmful lack of caution.

examples.everyday: Pulling out in front of that truck was reckless, so please slow down next time.
examples.professional: Deploying the model without testing it would be reckless, given the risk to our customers.
examples.analytical: A reckless ethic treats consequences as irrelevant, which makes it difficult to justify any action taken in their name.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds through a red light without looking: the danger is obvious, but the driver ignores it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English reccelēas, 'careless', from reck, 'to heed', plus -less.
common_mistakes: Using reckless for a mild mistake; it is stronger than careless and implies real danger.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'lees' instead of a reduced 'lus'.

reckless.etymology: From Middle English *rekles*, *reckeles*, *rekkeles*, (also *recheles*), from Old English *rēcelēas* (“reckless, careless, negligent”), equivalent to *reck* + *less*.

senses.definition: The act of defining an object (usually a function) in terms of that object itself.
senses.example: n! = n × (n − 1)! (for n > 0) or 1 (for n = 0) defines the factorial function using recursion.

senses.definition: The act of recurring.
The invocation of a procedure from within itself.
senses.example: This function uses recursion to compute factorials.

core.definition: A method of defining something, or solving a problem, by referring to smaller versions of the same thing, often through a function that calls itself.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the 'sion' ending is pronounced like 'zhun' as in 'vision.' Many learners say 'ree-KUR-shun,' which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, recursion is mostly used by programmers, mathematicians, and logicians. Non-specialists rarely use it, though people sometimes joke about recursion in a loose way. In technical settings, the term is used without hesitation.

distinctions.note: Iteration repeats steps with a loop; recursion solves a problem by calling the same procedure on smaller inputs.
Repetition is a general word for doing something again; recursion specifically refers to self-reference in definition or calling.
Recurrence means the act of happening again over time; recursion refers to self-referential definition or code.

examples.everyday: My kid thinks it's funny that a joke about a joke about a joke is a kind of recursion.
examples.professional: We fixed the bug by adding a base case to stop the recursion in the directory-traversal function.
examples.analytical: Gödel's proof relies on the recursion of self-reference, in which a statement is encoded so that it refers to itself.

nuance.analogy: Recursion is like a set of Russian nesting dolls: each doll contains a smaller version of itself until you reach the smallest one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin recursio, 'a running back,' from recurrere, 'to run back.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'shun' instead of 'zhun.'
Confusing recursion with recurrence, which means something happening again over time.
Using recursion as a synonym for iteration; they are related but distinct approaches.

recursion.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *recursiō* (“the act of running back or again, return”), from *recurrō* (“run back; return”), from *re-* (“back, again”) + *currō* (“run”).

senses.definition: Any of various elongate fish from the family Echeneidae, the dorsal fin of which is in the form of a suction disc that can take a firm hold against the skin of larger marine animals.
A serpent.

core.definition: A small fish that attaches to large sea animals such as sharks by a suction disc on its head.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, REM. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, and the final a is an uh sound, not a long ah. The r in American English is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biology term, though it can be used metaphorically for a parasite-like person.
nuance.usage_note: Remora is used mainly in marine biology, aquariums, and nature documentaries in the United States. In casual speech Americans would say suckerfish, which is a common name for it. Metaphorical uses exist but are rare.

distinctions.note: A shark is a large predator. A remora is a small fish that often rides on sharks, eating scraps and parasites.
A parasite lives on or in a host and harms it. A remora usually benefits from the attachment and does little harm.

collocations: a remora attached to a shark
hitching a ride like a remora

examples.everyday: At the aquarium, the guide pointed out a remora clinging to the side of the shark tank.
examples.professional: Our marine biology report describes the remora's suction disc as a key adaptation for feeding.
examples.analytical: The remora's attachment to larger animals raises questions about symbiosis, since the relationship is commensal rather than parasitic.

nuance.analogy: Like a passenger who hitches a free ride on a larger vehicle, staying close and getting carried along.
nuance.etymology: From Latin remora, meaning delay or hindrance, from re- and mora, delay.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final a as a long ah sound; it is uh.
Confusing remora with Remoras as a plural; the plural is remoras.

senses.definition: Synonym of pay back in all senses.
senses.example: I finally repaid my student loans, just before sending my kids to college.

senses.definition: To make worthwhile; to yield a result worth the effort; to pay off.
To give in return; requite.
To pay (cover with tar, pitch, etc.) again.

core.definition: To pay back money you owe someone, or to give something back in return for a favor, kindness, or harm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PAY, which is a long diphthong. The first syllable is a reduced vowel, so avoid saying 'ree' as in 'ree-PAY'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when you repay a kindness or debt, and it can be negative when you repay an insult or harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use repay for money, loans, and favors, as in 'I'll repay you Friday.' Repaying a favor is often done by doing something nice in return rather than by paying money. For casual talk, pay back is equally common, so the two are interchangeable in most everyday contexts.

distinctions.note: Pay back is more informal and common in speech, while repay sounds slightly more formal and is common in writing and finance.
Reimburse means an organization pays you back for money you already spent for them, such as work expenses.
A refund is money returned to you by a store or company, usually for goods or services you did not keep.

examples.everyday: Thanks for covering my lunch yesterday, I'll repay you on Friday.
examples.professional: The company must repay the bridge loan within ninety days of closing.
examples.analytical: Paul argues that a Christian cannot repay evil with evil, since vengeance belongs to God.

nuance.analogy: Repay is like returning a borrowed book to the library, giving back exactly what you received.
nuance.etymology: From Old French repaier, from re- 'back' plus paier 'to pay'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'repay to' the person instead of 'repay' the person directly, as in 'I will repay you' not 'repay to you'.
Confusing repay with reply or respond, which mean answering rather than giving back.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, repay refers both to human obligation and to God's justice. Romans 12:19 (RSV) says that vengeance belongs to God, who will repay, so believers should not take revenge themselves. Luke 14:14 (RSV) says that those who cannot repay a host will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. The Greek word behind repay in Romans 12 is apodidōmi, meaning to give back or render.

repay.etymology: From Old French *repaier* (“to pay back”), from *re-* + *paiier* (“to pay”), from Latin *paco* (“to settle, to make peaceful”), from *pāx* (“peace”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: Shining brilliantly; gleaming; radiant.
senses.example: The resplendent sun rose over the horizon.

senses.definition: Shiny and colorful, and thus pleasing to the eye; splendid in appearance.
senses.example: The peacock displayed its resplendent plumage.

senses.definition: Magnificent; glorious; splendid; marked by extraordinary excellence or beauty.
senses.example: The queen appeared in resplendent majesty.

senses.definition: Exhibiting the property of resplendency in Peano arithmetic.

core.definition: Very bright, shining and beautiful, in a way that is impressive and eye-catching.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPLEN. The final -ent is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'unt', and the ending does not rhyme with 'dent'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests splendor and admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'resplendent' mainly in writing, speeches or descriptions, such as in wedding toasts, church writing or literary prose. In casual talk, people say 'gorgeous', 'stunning' or 'dressed up'. Use it sparingly, because it can sound grand or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Splendid' is more general and can mean simply excellent; 'resplendent' stresses glowing appearance.
'Gorgeous' is casual and common; 'resplendent' is formal and suggests a more ceremonial beauty.

examples.everyday: Mom looked resplendent in her blue dress at the family reunion.
examples.professional: The conference hall was resplendent with the new brand colors, though the budget was tight.
examples.analytical: The poem describes the cathedral as resplendent, a word that makes its beauty a sign of divine order.

nuance.analogy: Like a stained-glass window with the sun behind it: the light makes the whole thing glow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin resplendere, 'to shine brightly', from re- 'again' and splendere 'to shine'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: say rih-SPLEN-dunt.
Using 'resplendent' in very casual speech, where it can sound overdone.

resplendent.etymology: From the obsolete sense of the English verb *splendish* (“to shine”), from Latin *splendere* (“to shine”), or from *resplend* + *ent*, from Latin *resplendere* (“to shine back, glitter”).

senses.definition: The sound made by a telephone when ringing.
A customizable tone used to indicate an incoming call on a telephone, especially a mobile phone.
senses.example: I set my favorite song as my ringtone.

senses.definition: Of a telephone: to play a ringtone.

core.definition: A sound or melody a phone plays to signal an incoming call, which the owner can usually choose or change.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light 'tone' that rhymes with 'phone.' Keep the 'ng' clean without adding a /g/ sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a casual, everyday word about personal phones.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ringtone' for both the sound and the act of choosing it. People often talk about changing a ringtone, and the word is common in casual speech and in phone settings. It is not used for landlines in most cases.

distinctions.note: 'Ring' can refer to the ringing sound itself, while 'ringtone' refers to the specific chosen sound on a phone.
A notification sound signals a text or alert, while a ringtone is specifically for incoming calls.

examples.everyday: My ringtone is so loud that people in the coffee shop turn around when I get a call.
examples.professional: Please put your phone on vibrate or silence your ringtone during the meeting.
examples.analytical: A ringtone is a small cultural marker that tells others something about the owner's taste and values.

nuance.analogy: A ringtone is like a doorbell that you choose yourself, so your home sounds like you.
nuance.etymology: Ring from Old English hringan and tone from Greek tonos, tension or pitch.
common_mistakes: Saying 'ring tone' as two words in formal writing, when 'ringtone' is standard.
Using 'ringtone' for a text alert sound, which is a different thing.

conversation.text: I changed my ringtone so I know when it's my wife.
Everyone checked their phones when the ringtone went off.
Your ringtone is so loud; can you turn it down?

senses.definition: An instance of wandering.
The ability to use a cell phone outside of its original registering zone.
The use of a network or service from different locations or devices.
Using the OS service of manipulating folders and documents from different PC devices by a registered user.

core.definition: Using your cell phone service in another area, city or country, often with extra fees from your provider.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ROH. The ending -ing is a short i sound, so it is 'ROH-ming' not 'ROH-meeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. In everyday use, it usually refers to extra charges that can be surprising.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear roaming when traveling abroad or when a phone signal switches to another carrier. Phrases such as 'roaming charges' and 'turn off data roaming' are common. Ask your carrier 'Does my plan include roaming?' A natural reply is 'Yes, but it's a few dollars a day.' It is mainly used in phone and data contexts.

distinctions.note: Wandering is physically moving around, while phone roaming is a technical service that connects your device to another network.
International calling is making calls to another country, while roaming is using your phone on a foreign network, which can apply to calls, texts and data.

examples.everyday: Turn off data roaming before we land, or the phone bill will be a shock.
examples.professional: Our travel policy covers roaming costs for approved trips, so submit receipts within thirty days.
examples.analytical: Roaming shows how mobile networks depend on interconnection agreements, which make a signal from one carrier usable on another.

nuance.analogy: Phone roaming is like a guest using a neighbor's Wi-Fi: it works, but the host may charge for it.
nuance.etymology: Derived from roam (verb), from Middle English romen, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'roaming fees' in casual speech when Americans more often say 'roaming charges'.
Confusing roaming with wandering, since the phone sense is technical and has nothing to do with walking.

conversation.text: Turn off data roaming before you land in Mexico, or you'll get a huge bill.
I got charged for roaming even though I barely used my phone.
My plan includes free roaming in Canada.

senses.definition: A citizen of ancient Rome or of the Roman Empire, a person whose status and rights were important in the New Testament.

core.definition: A citizen of ancient Rome or of the Roman Empire, a person whose status and rights were important in the New Testament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ROH, and reduce the second syllable to a schwa, 'mun.' Do not pronounce the final syllable as 'man' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in religious or historical contexts it names a people or citizen without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech Roman usually refers to a person from ancient Rome or from the Roman Empire, and it is common in history classes, Bible study, and museums. It may also describe modern people from Rome, Italy, but Americans usually say 'Italian' or 'someone from Rome.' Capitalize it as a proper noun.

distinctions.note: Italian refers to modern people of Italy, while Roman in this sense refers to the ancient Empire.
Latin is a language, while Roman refers to a citizen or person of the Roman state.

examples.everyday: My kid is doing a project on the Romans, so we visited the Roman ruins in town.
examples.professional: The grant proposal describes the infrastructure built by Roman engineers in the first century.
examples.analytical: Paul's status as a Roman citizen shapes the narrative in Acts, where his legal rights are repeatedly emphasized.

nuance.analogy: A Roman was like a citizen of a powerful empire whose passport protected them across the entire Mediterranean world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Romanus, from Roma, the city of Rome.
common_mistakes: Using lowercase roman for the people, which is a different word meaning a type of font or numeral.
Confusing Roman in the Bible with Romance or modern Italian identity.
